The NRC is also revising the definition of “potential ( printed page 69452) party” by removing references to subpart M of 10 CFR part 2, “Procedures for Hearings on License Transfer Applications,” which currently governs proceedings on license transfer applications. Many recent license transfer applications raise technical issues on decommissioning the Commission did not intend subpart M to address. Therefore, the NRC is eliminating subpart M and conducting license transfer proceedings under the more general provisions in subpart L of 10 CFR part 2, “Simplified Hearing Procedures for NRC Adjudications.”
Representation by Those Who Are Not Attorneys
For the reasons given in the Comment Response Document, the NRC has not adopted the limitations on non-attorney representation that were included in the proposed rule. Also, as discussed in a 2020 decision in the Vogtle proceeding (CLI-20-6, 91 NRC 225), the Commission has given greater latitude to hearing requests submitted by non-attorney intervenors while acknowledging that non-attorney petitioners are still expected to comply with our procedural rules. The NRC is clarifying that it is retaining this latitude for non-attorneys; however, this latitude is limited to construing the pleadings.
Requirements for Publication of Federal Register Notices Announcing an Opportunity To Request a Hearing, and Petition To Intervene
The NRC is making several changes to the regulations in §§ 2.101, 2.104, and 2.105 regarding the publication of Federal Register notices announcing an opportunity to request a hearing and petition to intervene. First, the NRC will generally notice these hearing opportunities as early as practicable. The hearing process may not reasonably be initiated before the NRC staff accepts the application for review ( i.e., dockets the application), but noticing the hearing opportunity as early as practicable thereafter would accelerate issue identification and resolution and could help mitigate any unavoidable delays that may occur later ( e.g., from illness of counsel or a witness). For certain proceedings, § 2.104(a) already requires the staff to issue the hearing notice “as soon as practicable after the NRC has docketed the application.” With one exception, the NRC is changing §§ 2.104 and 2.105 to expand this requirement to publish notices as soon as practicable to other Federal Register notices announcing a hearing opportunity in order to accelerate the initiation of the adjudicatory process, with a conforming change to § 2.101(f)(5). The exception pertains to notices of proposed action subject to the requirements of § 50.91 or 53.1515. Notices under § 50.91 or 53.1515 are for proposed amendments to specified production and utilization facility licenses. Historically, such notices have generally been published on a periodic basis given their volume. Given the high volume, it would not be practical to require individual Federal Register notices for these licensing actions. Also, only a small number of these amendments are challenged in the hearing process, and the associated licensing actions may be taken during the pendency of a hearing if the NRC makes a final no significant hazards consideration determination.
Second, the NRC is modifying §§ 2.104 and 2.105 to provide that Federal Register notices announcing a hearing opportunity must provide additional clarity by stating the Standard Hearing Completion Date specified in § 2.1207 and the additional filing deadline information required by § 2.309(b)(5). The basis for this change is described later in this notice in the context of changes to § 2.309 requirements for hearing requests, intervention petitions, and contentions.
Consistent with current practice, Federal Register notices will continue to state that prospective participants should notify the Secretary at least 10 days before filing a hearing request. While the agency recognizes this practice as helpful, in that it provides sufficient time to create an electronic hearing docket for a proceeding to facilitate compliance with electronic filing requirements and identify applicant and NRC staff contacts, imposing the practice as an additional requirement, as requested by one commenter on the rule, is not necessary. Outside the rulemaking process, the NRC will look to clarify notice templates to highlight the importance of meeting the requirements for electronic filing, including a timely request to establish a docket.
Meeting the licensing deadlines contemplated in the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 14300 will require strict adherence to the schedules described in the rule. Under existing § 2.307(a), time periods in 10 CFR part 2 may be extended either upon a showing of good cause or by stipulation of the parties. An extension of time by stipulation of the parties usually does not result in significant delay as the applicant and NRC staff have an interest in timely adjudication, and such extensions sometimes lead to more efficient resolution of issues ( e.g., an extension to complete consultation on a motion). However, contested extensions are more likely to lead to delay, and in recent years the NRC has sometimes found good cause for extensions based on requests detailing ordinary circumstances, such as general resource planning challenges.
The NRC has determined that no changes must be made to § 2.307(a), but in order to ensure that extension requests do not undermine timely adjudications, the NRC is reiterating the need for parties to clearly demonstrate good cause under § 2.307. Good cause is necessarily context specific, and the Commission has previously explained in its 2012 rule (77 FR 46562, August 3, 2012) that good cause in the context of § 2.307 should include “extraordinary circumstances.” Extraordinary circumstances are those events that are not within the parties' control, such as sickness or weather. Major holidays could similarly be an extraordinary circumstance. Thus, in normal circumstances the presiding officer should only grant an extension when a circumstance outside of the ordinary occurs that is not brought on by the movant's actions or inactions. In addition, under the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 14300, efficient and timely decision-making on license applications is a key focus area for the agency. Therefore, in circumstances where an extension request has the potential to extend an adjudicatory proceeding past the NRC staff's scheduled date to complete its review, the presiding officer should take into account schedule needs when making its determination and minimize the amount of time necessary to accommodate the circumstances giving rise to good cause.
Requirements for Hearing Requests, Intervention Petitions, and Contentions
The NRC is revising its regulations for hearing requests, intervention petitions, and contentions to (1) refine but not raise the contention admissibility criteria, (2) accelerate filing and decision deadlines consistent with the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 14300, (3) clarify and improve the requirements for hearing requests, intervention petitions, and new or amended contentions filed after the deadline in § 2.309(b) ( i.e., “challenges after the deadline”), and (4) provide clarity to participants on timelines, including when the reopening standards would apply to contentions raising new issues after the Standard Hearing Completion Date. However, as discussed in the Comment Response Document, this final rule is not adopting a provision in the proposed rule that would have ( printed page 69453) bifurcated filings and decisions on standing and contention admissibility (with standing being addressed on a more accelerated schedule), nor is the final rule adopting proposed § 2.309(k), which would have accelerated the filing of merits information on proposed contentions. As such, this final rule will not change current practice on these two matters: litigants will continue to address standing and contention admissibility in the same filings, the presiding officer will address both matters in the same decision, and litigants will not be required to file additional information on the merits of proposed contentions.
The NRC is also refining the contention admissibility criteria in two ways. First, the NRC is augmenting the requirement in § 2.309(f)(1)(iv) to demonstrate that a contention is material by requiring the petitioner to specify the legal requirement on which the contention is based. Specifying the pertinent legal requirement is important for demonstrating the materiality of the contention, and clarity in this regard can avoid needless confusion about the legal basis for a contention ( e.g., safety versus environmental requirements) and the inefficiencies that accompany efforts to resolve such confusion. Second, the NRC is revising § 2.309(f)(1)(vi) to require the petitioner to clearly indicate whether a contention is one of omission or adequacy. Different requirements apply to contentions of omission versus contentions of adequacy, and a lack of clarity regarding the nature of the contention requires additional resources from the NRC staff, applicant, and presiding officers to address.
As discussed previously, the NRC is taking a tailored approach to timeframes for initial filings and decisions thereon to account for specific types of applications rather than the more one-size-fits-all approach in the existing regulations, where the same time is provided for contentions on shorter or simpler applications as on longer or more complex applications. These tailored timeframes provide sufficient time for petitioners to meaningfully raise disputed issues in their hearing requests, for the applicant and NRC staff to file answers to hearing requests, and for the presiding officer to determine whether the standing and contention requirements are met.
Applying the tailoring approach described in the previous paragraph, this final rule includes the following schedules for hearing requests:
Under revised § 2.309(b), hearing requests and intervention petitions are due within set time periods after publication of theFederal Register notice announcing the hearing opportunity, depending on the type of application. As reflected in table 1, the NRC is retaining the existing standard 60-day filing period for Standard Proceedings, retaining the existing 20-day filing period for license transfer applications, providing a 30-day filing period for Expedited Proceedings, and providing a 45-day filing period for Focused Proceedings.
The NRC is retaining the existing 60-day filing period for hearing requests in Standard Proceedings because the pertinent applications generally present more complex technical issues than other license applications. The NRC is retaining the 20-day filing deadline for license transfer applications because this is a sufficiently expeditious period, and petitioners have demonstrated the ability to comply with this deadline over the last few decades.
The NRC is establishing a 45-day filing period for hearing requests in Focused Proceedings because the covered applications are generally less complex than applications within the Standard Proceeding category, as discussed previously.
The NRC is providing a 30-day hearing request period for the types of applications designated as Expedited Proceedings in this final rule—this provides sufficient time to evaluate and file hearing requests on these simple or narrow applications and meets the need for expedited decision-making on those applications. A 30-day period also ensures conformance with the 30-day notice provisions in AEA section 189 for proceedings on license and license amendment applications for production and utilization facilities under AEA sections 103 and 104b. and testing facilities under AEA section 104c.
These initial filing periods reflect the NRC's consideration of the need for timeliness and efficiency pursuant to the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 14300, as well as the anticipated length and complexity of the identified applications. This includes accounting for factors that would reduce the scope and complexity of the adjudicatory proceeding, such as whether an application for a production or utilization facility references a prior NRC approval providing issue finality in the adjudicatory proceeding that encompasses design issues.[6]
The NRC is also taking a tailored approach to the time provided for applicant and NRC staff answers to hearing requests and intervention petitions. Where the existing 60-day period for filing hearing requests is retained, the NRC is retaining the existing 25-day filing period for answers. Where the petitioner's filing period is reduced, the answer period would also be reduced, such that a 20-day answer period would correspond to a 45-day hearing request period, and a 15-day answer period would correspond to 30-day and 20-day hearing request periods. These reduced answer periods are 5 days shorter than the corresponding answer periods in the proposed rule, but as explained in the proposed rule, those proposed answer periods accounted for proposed § 2.309(k), which would have required an applicant's answer (and permitted the NRC staff's answer) to contain additional information on the merits of proposed contentions, including expert declarations. Since this final rule is not adopting proposed § 2.309(k), a modest reduction in the proposed rule answer periods is appropriate, and the due dates reflect the timeliness and efficiency goals in the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 14300 and the expected complexity of the proceedings. Finally, to avoid prejudice to the applicant and NRC staff, the NRC has clarified § 2.309(i) in this final rule so that the deadlines in § 2.309(i) for answers to hearing requests filed by the deadline in § 2.309(b) also apply to hearing requests filed by an approved extension to this § 2.309(b) deadline.
Consistent with existing regulations, replies to answers to hearing requests and intervention petitions submitted by the deadline in § 2.309(b) are due within 7 days of the answers.
These changes necessitate conforming changes to other regulations. For example, the NRC is removing the reference in § 54.27 to a 60-day filing period for hearing requests in power reactor license renewal proceedings because this final rule imposes a shorter filing period in such proceedings and because time periods for filing hearing requests should be specified in 10 CFR part 2 and not in other parts of the NRC's regulations. The NRC is also making other minor changes to § 2.309, ( printed page 69454) such as dividing § 2.309(a) into subparagraphs for clarity. In addition, the NRC is deleting the sentence in § 2.309(a) addressing proceedings under §§ 52.103 and 53.1452 to simplify the text and because that sentence is unnecessary given that other provisions of the NRC's regulations state that the Commission, acting as the presiding officer, will decide whether to grant hearing requests in proceedings under §§ 52.103 and 53.1452.
The NRC is retaining the existing filing periods for hearing requests, intervention petitions, answers, and replies in proceedings under subpart J of 10 CFR part 2, “Procedures Applicable to Proceedings for the Issuance of Licenses for the Receipt of High-Level Radioactive Waste at a Geologic Repository,” proceedings under § 52.103 or 53.1452, and proceedings under § 2.108(b)(2) on a denial of an application. As stated previously, this final rule is not intended to have more than a minimal impact on these types of proceedings. For clarity, the NRC notes that a demand for hearing in response to a denial of an application is not subject to the requirements of § 2.309 for hearing requests, and that a hearing request under § 2.108(b)(2) is subject to the requirements of § 2.309 because it comes from a person other than the applicant whose application was denied.
For all proceedings other than those under subpart J of 10 CFR part 2 or under § 52.103 or 53.1452, the NRC is modifying § 2.309(j) to impose accelerated deadlines for decisions by presiding officers on hearing requests submitted by the deadline in § 2.309(b). The decision will be due 30 days from the filing of replies in a transfer proceeding or Expedited Proceeding and 35 days from the filing of replies for other proceedings. Also, the § 2.309 deadlines for presiding officer decisions on hearing requests, intervention petitions, and contentions (including for such filings made after the filing deadline in § 2.309(b)) may be extended only if extraordinary circumstances prevent the presiding officer from issuing a decision by the deadline. Further, at the earliest practicable opportunity, the presiding officer would be required to notify the Commission and the litigants of the delay and the extraordinary circumstances that necessitate a delay. The potential need for oral argument, prehearing conferences, or additional briefing do not by themselves constitute extraordinary circumstances. Finally, while not addressed in the regulation text itself, the revised framework provides the presiding officers flexibility to take steps to accelerate the commencement of the evidentiary hearing phase, such as prioritizing issuance of decisions on admissible contentions.
The NRC is making several modifications to § 2.309(c) to clarify and improve the requirements for challenges after the deadline ( i.e., hearing requests, intervention petitions, and new or amended contentions filed after the deadline in § 2.309(b)). First, the NRC is clarifying and revising its regulations to avoid delays in making licensing decisions in certain proceedings due to the submission of challenges after the deadline that arrive near the end of the NRC staff's application review. Currently, petitioners must submit “motions for leave to file” contentions after the deadline that must satisfy § 2.309(c). Hearing requests and intervention petitions after the deadline must also satisfy § 2.309(c), although NRC regulations do not require a “motion for leave to file” such filings. The NRC is extending the “motion for leave to file” concept to hearing requests and intervention petitions after the deadline, and clarifying that challenges after the deadline would not be considered pending before the NRC until the motion for leave to file has been granted upon a showing of good cause under § 2.309(c). These changes address statutory requirements for a pre-effectiveness hearing (or pre-effectiveness hearing opportunity) for certain licensing actions.[7] For example, AEA section 189a.(1)(A) allows the NRC to issue operating licenses for certain facilities “in the absence” of a request for hearing from a person whose interest may be affected; therefore, the pendency of a hearing request before the NRC could affect the timing of the NRC's licensing decision. However, the AEA does not require a hearing request submitted after the specified deadline for hearing requests to be considered automatically pending before the NRC regardless of when it was filed. Rather, the related AEA section 189a.(1)(A) requirement specifying a 30-day notice period for operating licenses indicates that Congress contemplated that hearing requests be filed within specified periods.[8] The AEA provides no absolute right to file challenges after the specified notice period, nor does it indicate that petitioners may file challenges at any time they choose and thereby delay NRC action on the application. Under this change, challenges after the deadline would not be considered pending before the agency (and therefore would not delay NRC action on an application subject to a pre-effectiveness hearing requirement) unless and until the motion for leave to file the challenge after the deadline has been granted upon a showing under § 2.309(c) of good cause for filing after the deadline. Thus, as reflected in a new § 2.309(c)(7) and in revisions to § 2.340(i)(2), (j)(4), and (k)(2), the mere submission of such challenges after the deadline would not interfere with timely NRC licensing or regulatory decisions, even for those applications subject to a pre-effectiveness hearing (or pre-effectiveness hearing opportunity) requirement. The effectiveness of the licensing action in these circumstances would be stayed only if the petitioner meets the standard for granting a stay request.[9] To reflect the motion for leave to file terminology, the NRC is also making conforming changes in other paragraphs of § 2.309 and in §§ 2.4 (definition of “contested proceeding”) and 2.323(a).
Second, the NRC is modifying the timeline for motions for leave to file and associated challenges after the deadline. For the motion and challenge to be considered timely, they would need to be filed within 30 days of the new, materially different information giving rise to the challenge after the deadline. Currently, the regulations do not specify when the filing is considered to be timely, although 30 days is the time usually prescribed in presiding officer scheduling orders. This filing period would be accelerated to 20 days from the new, materially different information in transfer proceedings and ( printed page 69455) Expedited Proceedings because these proceedings are on a shorter timeline, and 20 days provides an appropriate period given the nature and scope of those proceedings. Because challenges after the deadline should be narrowly focused on new, materially different information, 15 days will be provided for answers to challenges after the deadline, consistent with the tailored approach to schedules described earlier. In addition, 7 days is provided for replies associated with challenges after the deadline, consistent with existing requirements. Finally, presiding officer decisions on challenges after the deadline will be due within 25 days of the reply, a deadline reflecting the anticipated narrower scope of challenges after the deadline. These deadlines for answers, replies, and decisions are reflected in new § 2.309(c)(5) and (6).
Finally, the NRC is modifying § 2.309(g) to reflect changes to § 2.310 that are discussed later in this notice, in particular the elimination of provisions in § 2.310(d).
The different timelines under § 2.309 for initial filings and decisions thereon for hearing requests and intervention petitions filed by the deadline in § 2.309(b)(1) and (b)(3) are reflected in table 1 (for simplicity, the table uses “hearing request” to refer to both hearing requests and intervention petitions). Table 2 provides the new timelines for motions for leave to file hearing requests, intervention petitions, and new or amended contentions filed after the deadline in § 2.309(b)(1) and (b)(3).
For clarity, the NRC is adding a new § 2.309(b)(5) (with cross-references in §§ 2.104 and 2.105) requiring Federal Register notices announcing an opportunity for hearing to specify the applicable filing deadlines for hearing requests, intervention petitions, and contentions (including those filed after the § 2.309(b)(1)-(b)(3) deadlines), and the applicable deadlines for the associated answers and replies. These notices will also be required to specify the Standard Hearing Completion Date for the proceeding, which is important information for application of the revised reopening requirements in § 2.326 and certain scheduling provisions in subpart L of 10 CFR part 2, as explained later in this notice.
As a result of this final rule, the NRC will use a revised hearing format in subpart L of 10 CFR part 2 to govern the adjudication of admitted contentions in almost all proceedings for the grant, renewal, licensee-initiated amendment, termination, or transfer of licenses or permits subject to 10 CFR parts 30, 32 through 36, 39, 40, 50, 52, 53, 54, 55, 61, 70 and 72. Subpart L is already used for most of these proceedings, but the NRC is increasing its use of subpart L with the following changes:
The NRC will conduct proceedings on a license to construct and operate a uranium enrichment facility under subpart L of10 CFR part 2 rather than subpart G of 10 CFR part 2 because the revised subpart L provides a faster, more streamlined process than subpart G and is better suited for licensing proceedings (in fact, most licensing proceedings are already conducted under subpart L). The NRC previously decided to conduct these uranium enrichment proceedings under subpart G because AEA section 193 requires such proceedings to be conducted “on the record” ( i.e., in ( printed page 69456) accordance with the formal procedures in the APA for “on the record” proceedings). The U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit subsequently concluded in 2004 (391 F.3d 338) that subpart L complies with these formal APA requirements. The revisions to subpart L continue to ensure that these enrichment proceedings comply with the formal APA requirements, while being more streamlined and efficient than the subpart G procedures. The NRC is also removing and reserving § 2.310(c) and revising § 2.700 to reflect this change.
The NRC is eliminating the provision in §§ 2.310(d) and 2.700 providing that certain proceedings for nuclear power reactors would be held under subpart G of10 CFR part 2 if (as stated in § 2.310(d)) “the presiding officer by order finds that resolution of the contention or contested matter necessitates resolution of issues of material fact relating to the occurrence of a past activity, where the credibility of an eyewitness may reasonably be expected to be at issue, and/or issues of motive or intent of the party or eyewitness material to the resolution of the contested matter.” This possibility has not been exercised since it was established in the 2004 Adjudications Rule (69 FR 2182, January 14, 2004), and subpart L of 10 CFR part 2 provides for cross-examination, if needed.
The NRC is removing and reserving § 2.310(g) and subpart M of10 CFR part 2, which currently governs license transfer proceedings, because the revisions to subpart L of 10 CFR part 2 suitably ensure that transfer proceedings are conducted promptly. As explained later in this notice, the streamlined and expedited subpart L procedures impose strict deadlines for completing license transfer evidentiary hearings in about 2.5 to 3.5 months. Also, subpart M is premised on the Commission serving as the presiding officer for transfer proceedings, but the NRC has decided to employ a Licensing Board as the presiding officer for transfer proceedings, as explained previously. The NRC is making conforming changes to reflect the removal of subpart M in § 2.4 (definition of “potential party”) and in §§ 2.313(a), 2.901, and 2.1103. In addition, the NRC is revising § 2.1103 to clarify the applicability of subpart K of 10 CFR part 2, adding a reference to 10 CFR part 52 to maintain consistency with the hearing format selection requirements in § 2.310, and providing, consistent with § 2.310(e), that subpart K would apply to the identified spent nuclear fuel storage capacity expansion proceeding upon the request of a party to use subpart K but that, otherwise, subpart L would be used.
The NRC is revising § 2.310(e) and removing and reserving § 2.310(h) to eliminate the option of using subpart N of10 CFR part 2 for licensing proceedings that would by default be conducted under subpart L of 10 CFR part 2 (absent those rare circumstances triggering the use of an alternative subpart). Subpart N was created to provide simplified procedures with oral hearings for the expeditious resolution of disputes. However, the NRC has never used subpart N since it was created in the 2004 Adjudications Rule (69 FR 2182, January 14, 2004), and the NRC believes that the oral hearing procedures for subpart N are generally not well suited for licensing proceedings, which often involve complex technical subject matter, where the precision of a primarily written hearing format is desirable.
To reflect these changes, the NRC is also making conforming changes to § 2.310(a). In addition, the NRC is removing cross-references in10 CFR parts 52 and 53 to specified subparts of 10 CFR part 2 as potential sources of hearing procedures for certain license applications. These cross-references are not consistent with this rule's changes to § 2.310, and hearing formats should be specified in 10 CFR part 2 and not in other parts of the NRC's regulations. The affected sections in 10 CFR part 52 are § 52.21 and 52.163 (appendix N to 10 CFR part 52, section 8 was considered an affected section in the proposed rule, but section 8 was subsequently removed from the regulations (91 FR 20063, April 15, 2026)). The affected sections in 10 CFR part 53 are §§ 53.1149 and 53.1285.
Timeline for Motions Submitted in Expedited Proceedings
Consistent with the overall streamlining approach of this final rule, the agency is amending § 2.323 to reduce the timelines for submittal of motions and corresponding answers in Expedited Proceedings. As previously discussed, Expedited Proceedings are simpler or narrower in scope and on a shorter timeline than typical proceedings covered under 10 CFR part 2. To achieve timelines commensurate with the substance and pace of Expedited Proceedings, § 2.323(a)(2) is changed to require that motions filed in these proceedings must be made no later than seven (7) days after the occurrence or circumstance from which the motion arises. Further, § 2.323(c) is amended to state that answers to motions in Expedited Proceedings must be submitted within seven (7) days after service of the motion. The agency is also instituting a simple restructuring of § 2.323(c) into three subparagraphs (1)-(3), introducing additional clarity and improving readability of the applicable requirements. Finally, in this final rule, the NRC is making an administrative correction to § 2.323(c) to change the title “Assistant Secretary” to the current title “Deputy Secretary.” The NRC is also making this correction in §§ 2.346 and 2.808.
The NRC intends to complete contested hearings on a schedule that supports licensing within the timelines contemplated by the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 14300. Consequently, to ensure that the adjudicatory process concludes within these timelines, the revised adjudicatory procedures have been constructed so as to generally accommodate an evidentiary hearing on admitted contentions filed by the § 2.309(b) deadline for filing contentions and a hearing on admitted contentions filed after that deadline, even if there is essentially no overlap between the filing and decision schedules for the two. To help accomplish this, the rule introduces a mechanism referred to as the Standard Hearing Completion Date, which facilitates the timely disposition of issues during the contested hearing process. The Standard Hearing Completion Date serves an important dual purpose in maintaining efficiency by identifying a time after which certain evidentiary hearing schedules are accelerated and, as discussed in the following paragraphs, defining a time when proposed contentions raising new issues must meet the standards for reopening the record.
The NRC acknowledges that in rare cases critical issues may arise late in a proceeding that might require the adjudication to exceed the NRC staff review timelines established in accordance with the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 14300. However, only critical issues should lead to such delays. Existing § 2.326 addresses this in part by requiring contentions filed after the record closes for an adjudicatory proceeding to meet the heightened reopening standards in § 2.326, which require the contention to be timely in accordance with § 2.309(c), address a significant safety or environmental issue, and demonstrate that it would likely materially affect the outcome of the proceeding. Under existing case law, the reopening standards would apply after the last live contention in the proceeding is resolved.
However, it is possible under existing precedent for a chain of periodically ( printed page 69457) filed new or amended contentions, none of them admissible, to hold open the record of the proceeding even to the end of the NRC's review of an application. To avoid this anomalous result and to provide a standard time for when the record would close to new issues for a proceeding, the revisions to § 2.326 add a new paragraph (e)(1) stating that the record for the proceeding will automatically close at the Standard Hearing Completion Date, a date providing sufficient time to hold an evidentiary hearing on admitted contentions submitted by the original deadline. The Standard Hearing Completion Date is based on the timeline structure of a particular proceeding, and applying the reopening standards to new issues raised after this date balances the rights of potential intervenors with the need for efficiency and predictability in a proceeding. The imposition of the reopening standards at this juncture in the timeline is intended to ensure that new issues submitted late in the proceeding are only admitted if shown to be critical, and would not affect litigation of issues already raised in a previously filed contention, as explained in subsequent paragraphs.
There may be instances in which an evidentiary hearing is completed before the Standard Hearing Completion Date. Consistent with existing practice, the presiding officer is expected to issue an order closing the record after the evidentiary hearing and before issuing the initial decision. In keeping with existing practice and consistent with themes underlying existing agency case law, § 2.326(e)(1) also provides that the record closes for the adjudicatory proceeding if the presiding officer enters an order closing the record following an evidentiary hearing but before the Standard Hearing Completion Date.
These revisions to § 2.326 comport with existing NRC precedent and are not intended to supersede the concepts already enshrined in case law. The Commission has routinely emphasized that the adjudicatory record for a proceeding closes at the conclusion of an evidentiary hearing, for example, in a 2012 decision in the Pilgrim proceeding (CLI-12-3, 75 NRC 132). Also, the Commission has applied the reopening provisions even earlier in a proceeding ( e.g., when a proceeding terminates once all contentions have been decided), such as in the Commission's 2012 decision in the North Anna proceeding (CLI-12-14, 75 NRC 692). Therefore, under existing precedent, the proceeding would terminate and the reopening provisions would apply in a situation when a presiding officer denies all hearing requests filed by the deadline in § 2.309(b) and there are no pending contentions in the proceeding.
The Commission has also recognized that if some issues are pending once the record closes, the record may remain open on those limited issues; an example is the Commission's decision in the Pilgrim proceeding (CLI-12-3, 75 NRC 132). This practice of keeping the record open for particular issues while closing the overall record for the proceeding has been supported in federal court in a 2013 decision in Massachusetts v. NRC (708 F.3d 63, footnote 18). Therefore, the new § 2.326(e)(1) also clarifies that if other contentions either remain pending or are subject to a motion for leave to file at the time the record closes, the record will remain open only with respect to the particular issues raised by those contentions. As a result, petitioners could continue to litigate live contentions filed prior to closure of the record under final § 2.326(e)(1) without having to meet the reopening standards. This would include (in certain narrow cases) filing proposed amendments of contentions on issues within the scope of the existing contention. For example, a petitioner may adjust an environmental contention filed on the application to address an NRC environmental document's discussion of the same particular issue, given that the NRC has the ultimate responsibility to comply with environmental laws and (when the NRC environmental document has been issued) the hearing on the issue would concern the adequacy of the NRC environmental document. Similarly, the reopening standards under final § 2.326(e)(1) would not apply to a contention of adequacy arising from new information mooting a contention of omission, where the contention of adequacy remains within the bounds of the bases set forth in support of the original contention. This aligns with well-established scope principles outlined in existing caselaw, such as the McGuire/Catawba proceeding (CLI-02-28, 56 NRC 373). However, reopening would apply to a new or amended contention filed after the record closure date under § 2.326(e)(1) that is not squarely within the confines of a live contention filed before that date ( e.g., if the pre-record-closure contention raised a particular environmental qualification concern for a component, a post-record-closure contention would have to meet the reopening standards if it raised a different type of environmental qualification concern for the component).
By providing the public with an opportunity to request a hearing prior to closing the record, this change comports with applicable Federal case law considering challenges to the NRC's reopening standards. In the 1984 decision Deukmejian v. NRC (751 F.2d 1287), the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit addressed a challenge to the NRC requiring an intervenor to meet the reopening standards to participate in a proceeding on a full power operating license in order to challenge an applicant's application to amend a low power license by extending the license term. The court determined the two actions were separate proceedings. By requiring the petitioner to meet the heightened pleading requirements in the reopening standard, the NRC improperly abridged the petitioner's hearing rights under section 189a. of the Atomic Energy Act. Thus, under Deukmejian, the NRC must provide petitioners with at least one opportunity to participate in an adjudication prior to closing the record. The revisions to § 2.326 meet this standard because they would not close the record until well after the opportunity to request a hearing expires.
Also, because the revisions to § 2.326 close the record in the specified circumstances, the NRC is revising §§ 2.104, 2.105, and 2.309(b)(5) to require Federal Register notices announcing opportunities to request hearings to state the Standard Hearing Completion Date for the proceeding. This will put the public on notice and provide additional clarity on record closure.
Further, to avoid any implication that final § 2.326(e)(1) overrides or otherwise annuls existing case law, the NRC is adding in response to comments a new § 2.326(e)(2) clarifying that, if the presiding officer enters an order closing the record following resolution of all live contentions in the proceeding, the record for the adjudicatory proceeding will close on the date specified in the order.
Finally, in addition to the adjustments described previously to address the scheduling directives of the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 14300, the agency is modifying the criteria included in § 2.326(a)(2) to state that a significant environmental issue under the National Environmental Policy Act can only be identified in a proceeding where a categorical exclusion listed in 10 CFR part 51 does not apply. The final rule language clarifies that categorical exclusions specifically pertain to the agency's obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act. In circumstances where a categorical ( printed page 69458) exclusion is used to comply with the National Environmental Policy Act, by definition, there are no significant environmental issues associated with the proposed Federal action under that statute. The agency considers this to be a clarity change responsive to the potential for increased use of categorical exclusions in future reviews. In another clarity change, the final rule specifically refers to categorical exclusions listed in 10 CFR part 51 because categorical exclusions in the regulations have issue preclusive effect in NRC proceedings.
The NRC is making several changes to reduce burdens to the parties from their obligations to make certain disclosures after contentions are admitted in most licensing proceedings and is also expediting the production of initial disclosures to support the accelerated evidentiary hearing timeframes in subpart L of 10 CFR part 2.[10]
The NRC staff's hearing file obligations are being entirely eliminated by this rule. Experience shows the hearing file currently required by § 2.1203 is burdensome and provides little value to the litigation because it covers the entire application under review instead of focusing on the admitted contentions. Moreover, the hearing file was established before the NRC required electronic filing of applications, regularly posted the entirety of applications and related documents on its website, and developed robust search functions in public-facing ADAMS. To the extent members of the public face difficulties in searching ADAMS, NRC Public Document Room staff are available to assist during business hours. Thus, the rationale supporting the hearing file obligation has become outdated. While the NRC is eliminating the hearing file requirements in § 2.1203, it is retaining paragraph (d) of this section, which specifies that no additional forms of discovery are authorized beyond what is permitted by subpart C of 10 CFR part 2.
In a change from the proposed rule, the NRC is retaining the NRC staff's § 2.336(b) disclosure obligations. While the staff's disclosures largely replicate the applicant's required disclosures or otherwise concern internal documents that are typically not produced to the other parties, there could be cases where the staff would disclose relevant information that would not otherwise be produced.
To effectuate the elimination of the hearing file requirement, the NRC is changing the scope of case-specific orders issued under § 2.307(c) for access to sensitive unclassified information. Under existing Commission precedent, these orders no longer apply to a petitioner if its hearing request is granted, as discussed in a 2010 decision in the South Texas Project combined license proceeding (CLI-10-24; 72 NRC 451, 461-63). That precedent, however, was issued when regulations required the NRC staff to disclose documents unrelated to the admitted contentions. Since the NRC staff would no longer produce a hearing file under § 2.1203, a change is needed so that a petitioner who is admitted as a party could continue to make requests for access under the § 2.307(c) access order on matters outside the scope of disclosures under § 2.336. The NRC intends to revise its templates for § 2.307(c) access orders to reflect this change; no change to the regulations is needed for this purpose.
The NRC is modifying the § 2.336(b) disclosures obligation in proceedings on denials of applications. In these types of proceedings, the staff is required to be a party and is in opposition to the applicant. The NRC is modifying § 2.336(b) to tailor the required document disclosures to the circumstances associated with a proceeding on a denial of an application ( e.g., the document categories associated with the application and NRC correspondence with the applicant would not apply because the applicant already would be in possession of this material). Finally, the NRC is making conforming changes to § 2.336(a) to reflect applicant disclosures in a proceeding on a denial of an application.
Second, the NRC is further modifying § 2.336 to reduce the burdens of other participants. Parties commonly agree to exclude from disclosures non-public draft documents that have not been circulated among the parties; the NRC is codifying this practice in the NRC's regulations in new subparagraphs (a)(4) and (b)(2). Moreover, in response to comments, the NRC is adding new subparagraphs (a)(5) and (b)(3) to exclude internal instant messages, text messages, and voice messages from mandatory disclosure absent a showing of exceptional circumstances. This exclusion only applies to communications that are internal to a party, its litigation team, and its contractors; if a single external person or entity is included in a communication, the communication would not be subject to this exclusion. These internal communications are generally high-volume, but low-value, and similar to non-public drafts that reveal a party's internal thinking. Generally, NRC licensing proceedings involve admitted contentions from qualified intervenors and focus on the technical conclusions on safety and environmental issues and how they are supported,[11] rather than on intent or motive that could be revealed through a party's internal thinking. Therefore, the NRC finds it appropriate to focus disclosures on technical documents that will reach the ultimate issues in dispute. However, to avoid inadvertently excluding relevant technical documents merely because they are attached to an excluded internal communication, the NRC is not excluding any documents attached to those excluded internal communications. These attachments would need to be included within the scope of mandatory disclosures if they are relevant to the admitted contentions. Also, in exceptional circumstances, such as when an admitted contention or license denial proceeding relates to a party's intent or motive and these types of internal communications would be relevant to the specific issue in the proceeding, the presiding officer may require that these communications be included.
Under existing rules, the duty to update disclosures relevant to an admitted contention ends when the presiding officer issues a decision resolving the contention. In this final rule, the NRC is also providing that the duty to update ends upon the initiation of the evidentiary hearing phase for the contention as delineated in an order from the presiding officer. This change serves to avoid requiring updates during the evidentiary hearing phase, as the relevant documents should have been disclosed by this point, and the evidentiary hearing is the most resource-intensive phase of the process.[12] Notably, this does not relieve ( printed page 69459) litigants from their ongoing general obligation to keep the presiding officer and litigants informed of relevant new developments in a proceeding, as the Commission emphasized in its 2006 decision in the USEC proceeding (CLI-06-10, 63 NRC 451).
Finally, the NRC is revising § 2.336(a) and (b) for added clarity and to require parties to produce their initial disclosures within 20 days of a presiding officer order admitting contested issues into the proceeding when the proceeding is immediately moving to the evidentiary hearing phase under § 2.332(d), while continuing to allow a 30-day period if the proceeding is not immediately moving to the evidentiary hearing phase or for an order granting a demand for hearing upon a denial of an application. Twenty days should be sufficient for diligent litigants to prepare their § 2.336 disclosures given the reduced scope of disclosures and modern discovery and file management tools, including artificial intelligence. Also, an accelerated initial disclosures schedule is necessary to support the expedited evidentiary hearing timeframes that are in the revised subpart L of 10 CFR part 2 when the proceeding is continuing to the evidentiary hearing phase immediately. In proceedings that are not moving immediately to the evidentiary hearing phase, i.e., when the expedited discovery schedule is not needed, the extra 10 days will allow parties additional time to meet their disclosure obligations.
The 20 or 30 days would generally run from the date of an order admitting contentions to account for new or amended contentions that might be admitted after the § 2.309(b) initial filing deadline for contentions. However, in a proceeding on a denial of an application, the 30-day period would run from the order granting a demand for hearing.
Conforming Changes to Scheduling Regulations
To accommodate the shorter timeframes for completing adjudications contemplated by this final rule, the NRC is making a number of conforming amendments to other sections in 10 CFR part 2, which pertain to scheduling. Specifically, the NRC is revising paragraph (b) in § 2.312, “Notice of hearing,” to reflect the Commission's expectation that considerations informing the selection of a time and place for a hearing should not override the overall timeframes established for timely adjudications by this rule or by any proceeding-specific Commission order. To provide additional flexibilities that may facilitate meeting those timeframes, the NRC is also revising § 2.329, “Prehearing conference,” to give the presiding officer or Commission discretion on whether to hold a prehearing conference.
Next, the NRC is making a number of edits to § 2.332, “General case scheduling and management,” to conform to the streamlined procedures and shortened timeframes elsewhere in this rule. Because the timeframes in this rule are mandatory, the NRC is revising paragraph (a) to reflect the presiding officer's obligation to develop a schedule that would meet the licensing timeframes in this rule. Likewise, the NRC is amending paragraph (d) to conform to the Commission's expectations that hearings under subpart L of 10 CFR part 2 would ordinarily begin once the presiding officer admits contentions, not when the staff issues its review documents. Specifically, the presiding officer would immediately proceed to an evidentiary hearing after the admission of a contention unless either (i) the NRC staff or applicant intend to seek dismissal or summary disposition of the admitted contention or (ii) the NRC staff decides to participate as a party but is not yet able to take final positions on the matters in controversy. Section 2.332(d) includes notification requirements to effectuate this provision—the proposed rule required these notifications within seven days of admission of the contention, but to avoid unnecessary delay, this final rule requires the notifications to be filed as soon as possible and no later than seven days after admission of the contention. The commencement of the evidentiary hearing phase would be delayed in cases where the NRC staff or applicant seek to resolve a contention through a motion to dismiss or a motion for summary disposition because the process for seeking dismissal or summary disposition is quicker and less resource-intensive than an evidentiary hearing; thus, the dismissal or summary disposition process may be a more efficient way of resolving a contention if the presiding officer decides that the standards for dismissing the contention are satisfied.[13]
The other reason for delaying the commencement of the evidentiary hearing—when the NRC staff seeks to participate as a party but is not able to take a final position on the matters in controversy—reflects the special role the NRC staff has in the licensing process and the Commission's desire to ensure that the presiding officer is aware of the NRC staff's considered position on the contested issues in those cases where the staff chooses to participate as a party. The NRC staff may not always be in the position (particularly early in its review of an application-specific or first-of-a-kind issue) to take a final position on the matters in controversy ( e.g., the NRC staff is seeking further information from the applicant or further considering information already provided). In this regard, the NRC staff is in a different position from the petitioner (who formulated and supported the proposed contention and should be in a position to commence the evidentiary hearing upon admission of the contention) and the applicant (who developed the application and should have the wherewithal to promptly address challenges to it). In the interest of prompt adjudication, revised § 2.332(d) further requires the NRC staff, in cases where it decides to participate as a party but is not yet able to take a final position on the admitted contention, to prioritize its resources to put itself in a position to provide testimony on the contention at the earliest practicable time and notify the presiding officer and the other parties when the staff is ready to do so.
Because the evidentiary hearing phase would, with certain exceptions, immediately commence after admission of a contention, litigants should ensure they are prepared to move immediately to an evidentiary hearing posture if a proposed contention is admitted. Thus, the NRC expects that litigants will consider their potential strategies and resource needs to litigate contentions at an evidentiary hearing before a presiding officer issues its decision on contention admissibility.
Section 2.332(d) is further revised to require the presiding officer, to the greatest extent practicable, to establish a schedule that will not extend past the ( printed page 69460) NRC staff's scheduled date for completing its review of the particular application. This provision has the purpose of ensuring timely NRC decision-making when it is practicable to do so and is intended to address both individual NRC reviews that are on a more expedited review schedule as well as the resolution of admitted contentions submitted later during an NRC review. In establishing a schedule under this provision, the presiding officer must ensure, as stated later in this rule, that the process still supports accurate decision-making and the development of a sound record, while giving parties a fair and equal opportunity to make their cases.
As a conforming change, the NRC is revising § 51.104(a) to remove the prohibition, in proceedings where a final environmental impact statement (EIS) has been prepared in connection with a proposed action, on the NRC staff either presenting a position on matters within the scope of the National Environmental Policy Act or offering the final EIS into evidence until the final EIS is made available. There is no statutory basis for this prohibition. Also, delaying the commencement of evidentiary hearings on environmental contentions until a final EIS has been completed, which might occur near the end of the NRC's review period, does not support the timeliness and efficiency goals of the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 14300. With the removal of this prohibition, the operative provisions of § 51.104(a) and (b) would be essentially identical, so the NRC is further consolidating § 51.104(a) and (b) into § 51.104(a) and removing and reserving § 51.104(b).
In another conforming change, the NRC is revising § 2.332(b) to reflect that only enforcement proceedings, not licensing proceedings, would be subject to the model milestones in appendix B to 10 CFR part 2. As discussed later, strict deadlines would be imposed in licensing proceedings rather than model milestones.
Finally, the NRC is amending § 2.334, “Implementing hearing schedule for proceeding,” by clarifying paragraph (a) to directly state the presiding officer's obligation to take necessary measures to ensure timely adjudication, by revising paragraph (b) to incorporate the standard in § 2.307(a) for extending a schedule and to incorporate an “extraordinary circumstances” standard for extending the deadline for completing an evidentiary hearing under subpart L of part 2, and by revising paragraph (c) to require the presiding officer to notify the Commission of any delays beyond the timeframes established by this rule.
Revisions to Hearing Format in Subpart L of 10 CFR Part 2 and Conforming Changes Elsewhere in Part 2
As explained previously, the NRC is making a number of significant changes to subpart L of 10 CFR part 2 to streamline and accelerate the hearing process for proceedings for the grant, renewal, licensee-initiated amendment, termination, or transfer of licenses or permits subject to 10 CFR parts 30, 32 through 36, 39, 40, 50, 52, 53, 54, 55, 61, 70 and 72. The two most significant changes are (1) to establish strict deadlines for the issuance of initial decisions in most licensing proceedings and (2) to provide greater flexibility to the presiding officer to decide which components of the subpart L hearing process are needed to support the presiding officer's decision-making. The NRC is also making other changes to streamline proceedings and ensure prompt and accurate decision-making, as discussed in the following paragraphs.
The NRC is establishing strict deadlines for the issuance of an initial decision to ensure that adjudicatory proceedings are promptly conducted to support the efficiency goals of the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 14300. These deadlines are tailored to different types of proceedings to account for the varying complexity of different license applications as well as the greater need for expedited decision-making in certain proceedings ( e.g., in Expedited Proceedings). These deadlines may only be extended if extraordinary circumstances necessitate a delay.
The NRC is also providing presiding officers greater flexibility in structuring the subpart L of 10 CFR part 2 evidentiary hearing phase because admitted contentions could take a wide variety of forms, and the presiding officer in an individual proceeding is better placed to decide what information is needed for the admitted contentions before it to support accurate decision-making and the development of a sound record, while ensuring that the parties are given a fair and equal opportunity to make their cases ( e.g., if one party may file written testimony and a position statement, all other parties would have the same opportunity). The presiding officer would also tailor the hearing schedule to the particular circumstances of a proceeding while complying with requirements for decision-making deadlines.
The specific changes to subpart L of 10 CFR part 2 and conforming changes elsewhere in this part are detailed in the following subsections for clarity and completeness.
A. Changes to Scope Provisions in § 2.1200
The NRC is revising § 2.1200 to reflect the modified scope of subpart L of 10 CFR part 2, as discussed previously in the context of changes to §§ 2.310 and 2.700. As stated before, license transfer proceedings will now be conducted under subpart L, as well as contested proceedings on the grant of licenses to construct and operate uranium enrichment facilities. The NRC is also clarifying § 2.1200 to reflect the existing provision in § 2.310(b) providing that enforcement proceedings may be held under subpart L if all parties agree.
B. Changes to § 2.1202 Regarding the NRC Staff's Authority and Role
The NRC is making several modifications to the provisions in § 2.1202 regarding the NRC staff's authority to take licensing actions and its role in the adjudicatory proceeding. First, the NRC is modifying provisions on the issuance and effectiveness of licensing decisions during the pendency of a hearing. Currently, § 2.1202(a) provides that the NRC staff is expected to promptly issue its approval or denial of the application, or take other appropriate action on the underlying regulatory matter for which a hearing was provided, and that the NRC staff's action is effective upon issuance except for several listed licensing actions. The NRC is revising the list of exceptions in § 2.1202(a) as follows:
Currently, the listed exceptions include all applications to construct and/or operate a production or utilization facility (including limited work authorizations and combined licenses). However, the pre-effectiveness hearing requirements in AEA section 189a. apply to production and utilization facilities licensed under AEA sections 103 and 104b. (corresponding to facilities under §§ 50.21(b) and 50.22 and10 CFR part 53) or testing facilities licensed under AEA section104c. (corresponding to a facility under § 50.21(c) that meets the definition of “testing facility” in § 50.2). The AEA's pre-effectiveness hearing requirements do not apply to production and utilization facilities licensed under AEA section104a. ( i.e., medical therapy facilities under § 50.21(a)) or to production and utilization facilities licensed under AEA section 104c. that are not testing facilities ( i.e., non-testing facilities under § 50.21(c)). The NRC is revising § 2.1202(a)(1) to reflect the scope of the AEA's pre-effectiveness ( printed page 69461) hearing requirements and in recognition of the lower safety significance of medical therapy facilities under § 50.21(a) and non-testing facilities under § 50.21(c).
The NRC is revising § 2.1202(a)(3) to remove the existing exception for10 CFR part 52 or 53 manufacturing licenses and put in its place an exception for licenses to construct and operate uranium enrichment facilities. In the 2007 rule adding the exception for manufacturing licenses (72 FR 49352, page 49420, August 28, 2007), the Commission acknowledged that there is no statutory requirement for including an exception for manufacturing licenses, but stated, “Nonetheless, as a matter of discretion, the NRC has decided to treat manufacturing licenses similar to construction permits in this regard, although the NRC reserves the right to change its practice in the future.” The NRC is removing the exception for manufacturing licenses because such licenses are not subject to the AEA's pre-effectiveness hearing requirements, a manufacturing license authorizes only the manufacture (not operation) of a facility, and vendors may fabricate major portions of a facility without a manufacturing license so long as those portions do not constitute a production or utilization facility. In these circumstances, there is no substantial reason to delay the issuance and effectiveness of a manufacturing license because of a pending hearing on the license application. The NRC is including an exception for applications for licenses to construct and operate uranium enrichment facilities. Such applications are currently subject to hearings under subpart G of 10 CFR part 2, but the NRC will now conduct contested hearings on these applications under subpart L of 10 CFR part 2. As stated previously, licenses to construct and operate uranium enrichment facilities are subject to a statutory pre-effectiveness hearing requirement, so it is appropriate to include them in the list of exceptions in § 2.1202(a).
The NRC is also modifying § 2.1202(b), regarding the role of the NRC staff in the hearing process, to accelerate the time in which the NRC staff is required to notify the presiding officer and the other parties of whether it will participate as a party in the proceeding, consistent with changes being made to § 2.332(d).
C. Changes to § 2.1203 Regarding Elimination of Hearing File
As discussed previously, the NRC is eliminating the hearing file requirements in paragraphs (a) to (c) of § 2.1203, while retaining the prohibition on additional discovery currently in paragraph (d) of § 2.1203.
D. Changes to § 2.1205 Regarding Summary Disposition
The NRC is making several changes regarding the schedule for summary disposition motions. First, to avoid unduly burdening parties as they undertake evidentiary hearing activities, the NRC is modifying § 2.1205(a) so that summary disposition motions are not permitted later than 30 days before the scheduled date for filing initial written testimony, absent permission from the Commission or presiding officer. Summary disposition may be a useful tool to avoid the resource expenditures associated with an evidentiary hearing, but after evidentiary hearing activities are underway, the filing of summary disposition motions risks distracting parties from their hearing preparations and burdening them unnecessarily.
Second, consistent with other changes in this final rule, the NRC is reducing the time for filing answers to summary disposition motions from 20 days to 15 days after service of the motion. The NRC also is providing a 20-day period from the filing of answers for a decision on the motion. Fifteen days should be sufficient for parties to address the pertinent standards for summary disposition motions, and a 20-day period for decisions is consistent with the overall hearing schedule and other timeframes for decisions in this final rule.
E. Changes to § 2.1206 to § 2.1210 Regarding the Hearing Process and Schedule
Currently, § 2.1206 to § 2.1210 provide the principal requirements for the subpart L evidentiary hearing process and schedule, including prescriptive requirements for which written filings are permitted and when, and whether an oral hearing must be held. For the reasons discussed earlier, the NRC is replacing these detailed requirements with simpler, more flexible, and more informal provisions for most proceedings. However, as reflected in an amended § 2.1206(a)(2), a hearing in a proceeding expressly required by the AEA to be determined on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing ( i.e., a proceeding for the grant of a license to construct and operate a uranium enrichment facility) will be required to comply with the APA's formal procedures for “on the record” hearings.[14] As explained in the following paragraphs, §§ 2.1206 and 2.1207 are completely revised, while §§ 2.1208 and 2.1209 are removed and reserved, and minor conforming changes are made to § 2.1210.
Under revised § 2.1206(a), the presiding officer would issue a scheduling order that would include the presiding officer's determinations on which written filings are permitted, the schedule for these filings, whether to hold an oral hearing, and the schedule for issuing an initial decision. Motions for cross-examination under § 2.1204 would be permitted (consistent with the existing regulations). Otherwise, the presiding officer would largely have flexibility to decide which written filings the parties would be permitted to make to provide the information necessary to support the presiding officer's decision. These potential written filings, which are listed in § 2.1206(b)(1), are (1) initial testimony, position statements, and supporting exhibits; (2) rebuttal testimony, position statements, and supporting exhibits; (3) motions in limine and motions to strike; (4) written briefing and/or written responses to questions from the presiding officer; (5) proposed questions for the presiding officer to ask the witnesses; and (6) proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law. These listed filings are currently available in a hearing process under subpart L of 10 CFR part 2, but the presiding officer would have flexibility to determine which filings to permit in a particular case. Similarly, the presiding officer would generally have flexibility to determine whether an oral hearing is needed to support the presiding officer's decision—currently, an oral hearing is required unless all parties agree to a hearing based solely on written presentations, but the NRC sees no need to require that an oral hearing be held as a default matter in all proceedings.
The initial decision is the culmination of the evidentiary hearing process, and the NRC is requiring that the scheduling order include the schedule for an initial decision, which must comply with the requirements of §§ 2.332 and (if applicable) 2.1207. As discussed later in this document, the amended § 2.1207 ( printed page 69462) provides schedule requirements for the issuance of initial decisions in most licensing proceedings.
Revised § 2.1206(b)(2) identifies certain additional flexibilities for the parties and the presiding officer that would apply depending on which written filings are permitted. Historically, written testimony in subpart L proceedings has been submitted in question-and-answer form, but a party would be allowed to submit testimony in affidavit form if the party prefers. Section 2.1206(b)(2) also provides that if statements of position and proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law are both permitted, parties would be allowed to file statements of position in the form of proposed findings and conclusions to facilitate the prompt preparation of proposed findings and conclusions after the hearing. Finally, § 2.1206(b)(2) clarifies the presiding officer's authority to allow oral motions in limine or motions to strike in lieu of (or in addition to) written filings. The amended § 2.1206(b)(2) does not provide an exhaustive list of flexibilities, and the presiding officer retains all authority provided in the pertinent provisions of 10 CFR part 2 to regulate the conduct of the proceeding.
The amended § 2.1206(c) retains requirements in existing subpart L of 10 CFR part 2 regarding the participants' ability to designate and present their own witnesses; the presiding officer's discretion to formulate and ask questions as the presiding officer considers appropriate; the presiding officer's authority to address situations where a witness is unable to appear in an oral hearing; and existing provisions on the propounding of questions by the presiding officer and the submission of proposed questions for the presiding officer to ask the witnesses.
While the presiding officer would ordinarily have great flexibility to structure the evidentiary hearing, for two types of proceedings—a proceeding expressly required by the AEA to be determined on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing ( i.e., a proceeding on an application to construct and operate a uranium enrichment facility) and a proceeding on a denial of an application—revised § 2.1206(d) requires (consistent with existing subpart L of 10 CFR part 2) that (1) a transcribed oral hearing be held unless all parties jointly agree to dispense with an oral hearing, and (2) each party be permitted to file written testimony, a position statement, and supporting exhibits; to submit rebuttal evidence and argument; and to file proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law. These elements of an evidentiary hearing are required for a proceeding concerning the grant of a license to construct and operate a uranium enrichment facility to maintain consistency with the requirements for formal “on the record” hearings in the APA.[15] The NRC is also retaining these elements of a subpart L hearing for denials of applications because hearings on denials ordinarily arise from a “demand for hearing” under § 2.103 or 2.108 that would not typically involve the robust issue development provided in the initial filings under the § 2.309 process.[16]
The NRC is providing scheduling requirements in § 2.1207 for issuance of initial decisions in proceedings under subpart L, with the exception of enforcement proceedings and proceedings on denials of applications.[17] For each type of proceeding, § 2.1207 includes (1) a deadline for initial decisions for contentions, including (as applicable) a shorter deadline for initial decisions on contentions submitted after the Standard Hearing Completion Date, (2) a specification of the Standard Hearing Completion Date for that type of proceeding, and (3) a requirement that extraordinary circumstances are necessary for delays beyond the deadline for initial decision. Deadlines are stated in terms of calendar days from the admission of the contention, assuming that the presiding officer immediately proceeds to an evidentiary hearing in accordance with § 2.332(d), although if this does not occur ( e.g., the NRC staff is not yet able to take a final position on the contested issues, the applicant seeks to resolve the admitted contention through a summary disposition motion) the deadline would run from an alternative triggering event established in the scheduling order ( e.g., the NRC staff's notification that it is able to take a final position on the contested issues, a presiding officer order denying or partially denying an applicant summary disposition motion).Also, in accordance with changes to § 2.334(c) discussed previously, the presiding officer must provide written notification to the Commission any time during the course of the proceeding when it appears that the issuance of the initial decision will be delayed beyond the time specified in the hearing schedule.
In establishing deadlines, the NRC considered the anticipated complexity of the pertinent application, along with associated NRC review deadlines and goals. More time is given for the Standard Proceeding applications subject to an 18-month standard NRC review schedule, while less time is given for less complex applications. While the complexity of the issues admitted for hearing in a particular proceeding will depend on case-specific factors, more complex applications have the potential for more complex contested issues, which is a factor to be considered in establishing these general evidentiary hearing deadlines in the regulations. However, if a less complex dispute is amenable to a shorter process, the Licensing Board should account for that in its schedule for an individual proceeding.
In some cases, the NRC has not established a standard review schedule shorter than 18 months for a particular application, but the NRC would seek to come to a final decision in substantially less than 18 months, if practical, because the application review is less complicated or of narrower scope ( e.g., a 10 CFR part 52 commercial reactor application referencing an issued design certification, which finally resolves most design issues for both the staff review and the adjudicatory proceeding). The deadlines in final § 2.1207 account for these circumstances.
The NRC has also considered different timelines depending on when the contention was submitted. For two reasons, the NRC is generally establishing a shorter deadline for initial decisions on contentions submitted after the Standard Hearing Completion Date. First, an expedited schedule is needed for admitted contentions submitted later in a proceeding to support prompt NRC decision-making consistent with the ( printed page 69463) direction in the ADVANCE Act and E.O. 14300. As stated previously and discussed in more detail later in the context of table 4, the NRC's general overall goal with these changes has been to establish a process where two non-overlapping hearings could be held within the 18-month and 1-year E.O. 14300 deadlines (one hearing on contentions submitted by the § 2.309(b) deadline—as reflected in the calculation of the Standard Hearing Completion Date—and the second hearing on a new or amended contention submitted after the Standard Hearing Completion Date). Second, consistent with other changes to 10 CFR part 2 in this final rule (in particular, those in § 2.332(d)), the NRC would ordinarily proceed to an evidentiary hearing on contentions submitted earlier in the proceeding as soon as practicable. Thus, hearings on admitted contentions submitted later in the proceeding would be expected to narrowly focus on new information arising later in the review, in contrast to contentions submitted early in the review that might embrace the entire application. To promote clarity, § 2.1207 specifies the Standard Hearing Completion Date for different types of proceedings, based on the new definition of this term in § 2.4, and the Standard Hearing Completion Date for a particular proceeding would be specified in the Federal Register notice announcing the hearing opportunity, in accordance with this rule's revisions to §§ 2.104, 2.105, and 2.309. The Standard Hearing Completion Dates in this final rule reflect changes to proposed rule scheduling provisions discussed elsewhere in this notice; also, the NRC has corrected an omission in the proposed rule by including a separate Standard Hearing Completion Date in final § 2.1207(d) for transfer proceedings other than those for a license authorizing operation of a reactor.
Regarding the specific deadlines in § 2.1207, the NRC is establishing in § 2.1207(a) the longest deadline (135 days) for the Standard Proceeding applications ( i.e., those that, as described previously, are subject to a 60-day filing period for hearing requests). The NRC determined this 135-day deadline by establishing a reasonable, hypothetical schedule for conducting a formal APA hearing in a Standard Proceeding for a license to construct and operate a uranium enrichment facility. While the presiding officer has flexibility to establish a hearing schedule based on the specific circumstances of a proceeding, the hypothetical schedule that follows in table 3 shows that 135 days is sufficient time to conduct an evidentiary hearing that includes initial and rebuttal testimony and statements of position, an oral hearing, and post-hearing proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law. A shorter deadline (100 days) is provided for hearings on contentions submitted after the Standard Hearing Completion Date, for the reasons given previously and as supported by the hypothetical timeline in table 3. These initial decision deadlines, combined with the associated timetables for initial filings identified in tables 1 and 2, support the ability to resolve contested adjudicatory issues within the NRC's standard 18-month review schedules for these enrichment applications with substantial margin, as shown in table 4.
In the proposed rule, the NRC had proposed shorter evidentiary hearing deadlines for other applications in the Standard Proceeding category, but these deadlines were largely premised on the submission of additional merits information in the initial filings under proposed § 2.309(k). Proposed § 2.309(k) was intended to expedite the evidentiary hearing through the development of additional merits information up front that could be used for the evidentiary hearing and would also enlighten the litigants as to the merits positions of the other parties. Under proposed § 2.309(k), the litigants would generally have been further along in developing their initial testimony and position statements and could have saved additional time and resources by focusing these filings on the merits positions of the other parties. Since this final rule does not adopt the provisions in proposed § 2.309(k), the NRC is adjusting the evidentiary hearing schedules to provide a modest amount of additional time for the parties to prepare their initial testimony and position statements given the absence of information that would have been developed and disclosed under proposed § 2.309(k). Therefore, the NRC is modestly increasing the evidentiary hearing schedules for the other Standard Proceeding applications to account for this change, as discussed in the Comment Response Document. Specifically, the NRC is applying the deadlines discussed previously for formal enrichment proceedings to the completion of evidentiary hearings for other applications in the Standard Proceeding category. Both types of applications are subject to similar NRC review schedules and can involve litigation of more complex nuclear safety issues. While these other Standard Proceeding applications are not subject to the formal APA hearing requirements as a matter of law, any adjustments the NRC might make because of this difference would not be sufficiently large to justify the complexity of a different hearing timeline. The NRC has not developed a hypothetical timeline for the non-enrichment evidentiary hearings because the presiding officer has greater flexibility on how to structure these ( printed page 69465) proceedings, as they are not subject to the formal APA hearing requirements.
Section 2.1207(b) prescribes initial decision deadlines for Expedited Proceedings where the application references both (i) a categorical exclusion listed in 10 CFR part 51, and (ii) an NRC approval providing finality in the adjudicatory proceeding on design information within the application (including a design certification or a manufacturing license). In such cases, the potential adjudicatory issues should be narrow in scope.
